segments.text: Finally, a beautifully simple rule ties absorbing and emitting together.
Place a shiny polished can and a black-painted can of boiling water side by side. The black one cools noticeably faster. Why?
Because good absorbers of radiation are also good emitters. A surface that greedily soaks up radiation also pours it out greedily.
That is Kirchhoff's law, and numerically it means emissivity equals absorptivity for a surface at a given temperature.
The ideal limit is a black body: one that absorbs all radiation falling on it, reflecting and transmitting none, and therefore emits at the maximum possible rate for its temperature.
No real surface is perfectly black, but a small hole in a closed cavity comes astonishingly close — a ray entering bounces around inside and is absorbed before it can escape.
This is also why a thermos flask defeats all three modes at once: silvered walls reflect radiation, and the vacuum gap kills conduction and convection.
आख़िर में, एक ख़ूबसूरत सीधा rule सोखने और छोड़ने को जोड़ देता है।
एक चमकीला polished can और एक काला painted can, दोनों उबलते पानी के, साथ रखो। काला वाला साफ़ तेज़ी से ठंडा होता है। क्यों?
क्योंकि radiation के अच्छे absorbers, अच्छे emitters भी होते हैं। जो सतह लालच से radiation सोखती है, लालच से उगलती भी है।
यही Kirchhoff's law है, और संख्या में इसका मतलब — किसी सतह के लिए दिए temperature पर emissivity बराबर absorptivity।
Ideal हद है black body: जो उस पर गिरती सारी radiation सोख ले, न reflect न transmit, और इसलिए अपने temperature पर maximum rate से emit करे।
कोई असली सतह पूरी काली नहीं, पर बंद cavity में एक छोटा छेद हैरतअंगेज़ रूप से क़रीब आता है — अंदर घुसी किरण घूमती रहती है और भागने से पहले सोख ली जाती है।
इसीलिए thermos flask तीनों modes एक साथ हरा देता है: चाँदी जैसी दीवारें radiation reflect करती हैं, और vacuum gap conduction व convection ख़त्म करता है।

sections.title: The fine print: emissivity, net exchange, Newton's approximation

board_events.text: Real surfaces and the small-excess limit
Pure Stefan (E = sigma T-to-the-4) is for a perfect black body.
Net exchange: subtract what the surroundings radiate back.
Newton's cooling — rate proportional to excess — holds for a small gap.
It is Stefan's law in disguise, valid only near the surroundings.

segments.text: Before the formulas, the fine print that separates a memoriser from someone who understands.
Stefan's law in its pure form, E equals sigma T to the fourth, holds for a perfect black body.
For a real surface we insert the emissivity e, a number between zero and one, and write power equals e sigma A T to the fourth.
But a warm body sits in surroundings that radiate back at it, so what matters is the net — subtract the surroundings' contribution.
Net power equals e sigma A times T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, where T naught is the surroundings' temperature.
And Newton's law of cooling — that the rate of cooling is proportional to the temperature excess — is only an approximation, valid when that excess is small.
As we will prove, it is just Stefan's T-to-the-fourth law in disguise for a small excess — for a large difference, the full fourth-power behaviour takes over.
Formulas से पहले, वो बारीक शर्तें जो रटने वाले को समझने वाले से अलग करती हैं।
Stefan's law अपने शुद्ध रूप में, E बराबर sigma T to the fourth, एक perfect black body के लिए है।
असली सतह के लिए हम emissivity e डालते हैं, zero और one के बीच एक संख्या, और लिखते हैं power बराबर e sigma A T to the fourth।
पर गरम body उन surroundings में है जो वापस उस पर radiate करती हैं, तो जो मायने रखता है वो net है — surroundings का हिस्सा घटाओ।
Net power बराबर e sigma A गुना T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, जहाँ T naught surroundings का temperature।
और Newton's law of cooling — कि cooling की rate temperature excess के proportional है — सिर्फ़ एक approximation है, तब valid जब वो excess छोटा हो।
जैसा हम साबित करेंगे, यह बस छोटे excess के लिए Stefan के T-to-the-fourth law का भेस है — बड़े फ़र्क़ के लिए पूरी fourth-power behaviour हावी हो जाती है।

sections.title: Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien

board_events.text: Stefan-Boltzmann and Wien
e emissivity (0 to 1); sigma = 5.67e-8 W per m sq per K to the 4.
Wien's constant b = 2.9e-3 m K; hotter means a smaller peak wavelength.
Always use absolute kelvin — the fourth power magnifies any error.

segments.text: Let us write the two radiation laws cleanly.
Stefan-Boltzmann: power equals e sigma A T to the fourth, and net power equals e sigma A times T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth.

Here e is emissivity, between zero and one, one for a black body; and sigma, the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, is five point six seven times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth.
For a black body, the emissive power per unit area is simply sigma T to the fourth.
Wien's displacement law: lambda m times T equals b, where lambda m is the wavelength of peak emission.
Wien's constant b is two point nine times ten to the minus three metre kelvin. A hotter body means a smaller peak wavelength — bluer.
<whisper> And the golden rule for both: always work in absolute kelvin. With a fourth power, a stray use of Celsius wrecks the answer.
चलो दोनों radiation laws साफ़ लिखें।
Stefan-Boltzmann: power बराबर e sigma A T to the fourth, और net power बराबर e sigma A गुना T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth।

यहाँ e है emissivity, zero और one के बीच, black body के लिए one; और sigma, Stefan-Boltzmann constant, है five point six seven times ten to the minus eight watts per square metre per kelvin to the fourth।
Black body के लिए, per unit area emissive power बस sigma T to the fourth है।
Wien's displacement law: lambda m गुना T बराबर b, जहाँ lambda m peak emission की wavelength।
Wien's constant b है two point nine times ten to the minus three metre kelvin। ज़्यादा गरम body मतलब छोटी peak wavelength — नीली।
<whisper> और दोनों के लिए golden rule: हमेशा absolute kelvin में काम करो। चौथी power के साथ, Celsius की एक भूल answer बिगाड़ देती है।

sections.title: Kirchhoff, Newton's cooling, and the black body

board_events.text: Kirchhoff and Newton's cooling
Emissivity = absorptivity: good absorbers are good emitters.
k depends on area, surface, and specific heat; T-naught is surroundings.
Black body: absorbs all (absorptivity 1), emits the maximum at every wavelength.

segments.text: Two more relations complete the toolkit: Kirchhoff, and Newton's law of cooling.
Kirchhoff's law: at a given temperature, the ratio of emissive power to absorptive power is the same for all bodies, and equals the emissive power of a black body.
The practical reading is short: emissivity equals absorptivity — good absorbers are good emitters.
Newton's law of cooling: minus d T by d t equals k times T minus T naught, for a small temperature excess.
The constant k depends on the body's area, the nature of its surface, and its specific heat; T naught is the surroundings' temperature.
The practical average form, for a body cooling from T one to T two in time t, uses the mean temperature: T one minus T two over t equals k times the average of T one and T two, minus T naught.
And the black body, once more: it absorbs all incident radiation, absorptivity one, and emits the maximum possible at every wavelength.
दो और relations toolkit पूरी करती हैं: Kirchhoff, और Newton's law of cooling।
Kirchhoff's law: दिए temperature पर, emissive power का absorptive power से अनुपात सभी bodies के लिए एक-सा है, और black body की emissive power के बराबर।
व्यावहारिक मतलब छोटा है: emissivity बराबर absorptivity — अच्छे absorbers अच्छे emitters।
Newton's law of cooling: minus d T by d t बराबर k गुना T minus T naught, छोटे temperature excess के लिए।
Constant k, body के area, उसकी सतह की क़िस्म, और specific heat पर निर्भर; T naught surroundings का temperature।
व्यावहारिक average रूप, T one से T two तक time t में ठंडे होते body के लिए, mean temperature use करता है: T one minus T two बटा t बराबर k गुना T one और T two का average, minus T naught।
और black body, एक बार फिर: यह सारी incident radiation सोखता है, absorptivity one, और हर wavelength पर maximum possible emit करता है।

sections.title: Deriving Newton's cooling from Stefan's law

board_events.text: Newton's cooling from Stefan's law
Write $T=T_0+\Delta T$ with $\Delta T$ small, then expand the fourth power.
So $k=\dfrac{4e\sigma A T_0^3}{mc}$ — an approximation valid only for a small excess.

segments.text: Here is the most-asked derivation of the subtopic: Newton's cooling is really Stefan's law for a small excess.
Start from the net rate of energy loss by Stefan's law: net power equals e sigma A times T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth.
This loss comes out of the body's internal energy, so minus m c d T by d t equals that same e sigma A bracket.
Now write T as T naught plus delta T, with delta T small, and expand T to the fourth by the binomial approximation.
Keeping only the first-order term, T to the fourth is about T naught to the fourth plus four T naught cubed delta T, so the difference is about four T naught cubed delta T.
Substitute back: minus d T by d t equals four e sigma A T naught cubed over m c, times T minus T naught — exactly k times T minus T naught.
<excited> So the cooling constant is four e sigma A T naught cubed over m c — and the derivation reveals the law is only an approximation, valid while the excess is small.
यह इस subtopic का सबसे ज़्यादा पूछा derivation है: Newton's cooling असल में छोटे excess के लिए Stefan's law है।
Stefan's law से energy खोने की net rate से शुरू करो: net power बराबर e sigma A गुना T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth।
यह loss body की internal energy से आता है, तो minus m c d T by d t बराबर वही e sigma A bracket।
अब T को T naught plus delta T लिखो, delta T छोटा, और T to the fourth को binomial approximation से expand करो।
सिर्फ़ first-order term रखते हुए, T to the fourth लगभग T naught to the fourth plus four T naught cubed delta T, तो फ़र्क़ लगभग four T naught cubed delta T।
वापस substitute: minus d T by d t बराबर four e sigma A T naught cubed बटा m c, गुना T minus T naught — ठीक k गुना T minus T naught।
<excited> तो cooling constant है four e sigma A T naught cubed बटा m c — और derivation दिखाता है कि यह law सिर्फ़ approximation है, तब valid जब excess छोटा हो।

segments.text: A clean board numerical on net radiation.
A spherical black body of radius five centimetres is held at three hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius, in surroundings at twenty seven. Find the net power it radiates.
First convert to kelvin: the body is six hundred kelvin, the surroundings three hundred. The radius is zero point zero five metres, and being black, emissivity is one.
Surface area is four pi r squared: four pi times zero point zero five squared, about three point one four times ten to the minus two square metres.
The fourth-power difference: six hundred to the fourth minus three hundred to the fourth is one point two one five times ten to the eleven.
So net power is sigma, times area, times that difference — about two hundred sixteen watts.
Two habits to keep: convert temperatures to kelvin before the fourth power, and never drop the T naught to the fourth term — the surroundings radiate back.
Net radiation पर एक साफ़ board numerical।
पाँच centimetre radius का एक spherical black body three hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius पर रखा है, surroundings twenty seven पर। यह जो net power radiate करता है निकालो।
पहले kelvin में बदलो: body six hundred kelvin, surroundings three hundred। Radius zero point zero five metres, और काला होने से emissivity one।
Surface area है four pi r squared: four pi गुना zero point zero five squared, लगभग three point one four times ten to the minus two square metres।
Fourth-power का फ़र्क़: six hundred to the fourth minus three hundred to the fourth है one point two one five times ten to the eleven।
तो net power है sigma, गुना area, गुना वो फ़र्क़ — लगभग two hundred sixteen watts।
दो आदतें रखो: चौथी power से पहले temperatures kelvin में बदलो, और T naught to the fourth term कभी मत छोड़ो — surroundings वापस radiate करती हैं।

segments.text: A two-error trap that catches students constantly.
The absolute temperature of a body is raised from twenty seven degrees Celsius to three hundred twenty seven. By what factor does the power it radiates increase?
The trap is double: students plug the Celsius numbers, or they forget the fourth power and answer two. Both are wrong.
Convert to kelvin first: three hundred to six hundred, a ratio of exactly two.
Since power is proportional to T to the fourth, the ratio of powers is the ratio of temperatures, to the fourth: two to the fourth, which is sixteen.
Notice we never touched sigma or the area — a pure ratio in kelvin does the whole job.
Work in kelvin and use the ratio to the fourth. Forgetting to convert Celsius to kelvin is the single deadliest trap here, because the fourth power magnifies the error enormously.
एक दो-ग़लती वाला trap जो students को लगातार फँसाता है।
एक body का absolute temperature twenty seven degrees Celsius से three hundred twenty seven तक बढ़ाया जाता है। यह जो power radiate करता है किस factor से बढ़ती है?
Trap दुगना है: students Celsius numbers डालते हैं, या fourth power भूलकर answer देते हैं two। दोनों ग़लत।
पहले kelvin में बदलो: three hundred से six hundred, ठीक two का ratio।
चूँकि power, T to the fourth के proportional है, powers का ratio है temperatures के ratio का, to the fourth: two to the fourth, यानी sixteen।
ध्यान दो हमने sigma या area को छुआ ही नहीं — kelvin में एक शुद्ध ratio सारा काम कर देता है।
Kelvin में काम करो और ratio to the fourth use करो। Celsius को kelvin में बदलना भूलना यहाँ सबसे ख़तरनाक trap है, क्योंकि चौथी power ग़लती को ज़बरदस्त बढ़ा देती है।

segments.text: This one combines both laws in sequence, the standard astrophysics-flavoured question.
A star's radiation peaks in intensity at five hundred nanometres. Treating it as a black body, find its surface temperature and the power it radiates per unit area.
Step one is Wien: temperature is Wien's constant b divided by the peak wavelength.
So T is two point nine times ten to the minus three, over five hundred times ten to the minus nine — which comes to five thousand eight hundred kelvin.

Step two is Stefan, per unit area: E equals sigma T to the fourth — five point six seven times ten to the minus eight, times fifty eight hundred to the fourth — about six point four times ten to the seven watts per square metre.
So the pattern is two clean steps: Wien to get temperature from the spectrum, then Stefan to get the power — the standard astrophysics-flavoured J E E Main question.
Notice the temperature landing near five thousand eight hundred kelvin, which is indeed close to the Sun's own surface temperature.
यह दोनों laws को क्रम से जोड़ता है, standard astrophysics वाला question।
एक star की radiation five hundred nanometres पर सबसे तेज़ होती है। इसे black body मानकर, इसका surface temperature और per unit area radiate power निकालो।
Step one है Wien: temperature बराबर Wien's constant b बटा peak wavelength।
तो T है two point nine times ten to the minus three, बटा five hundred times ten to the minus nine — जो बनता है five thousand eight hundred kelvin।

Step two है Stefan, per unit area: E बराबर sigma T to the fourth — five point six seven times ten to the minus eight, गुना fifty eight hundred to the fourth — लगभग six point four times ten to the seven watts per square metre।
तो pattern है दो साफ़ steps: Wien से spectrum से temperature, फिर Stefan से power — standard astrophysics वाला J E E Main question।
ध्यान दो temperature five thousand eight hundred kelvin के पास आया, जो सचमुच Sun की अपनी सतह के temperature के क़रीब है।

segments.text: Our advanced example shows the character of Newton's cooling right in the numbers.
A metal block cools from eighty to sixty degrees in five minutes, in a room at twenty. How long to cool further, from sixty to forty?
Use the average-temperature form, taking the mean temperature of the block during each interval.
First stage: eighty minus sixty over five equals k times the average seventy, minus twenty. So four equals fifty k, giving k equals zero point zero eight per minute.
Second stage uses the same k, with mean temperature now fifty: sixty minus forty over t equals zero point zero eight times thirty, which is two point four.
So twenty over t equals two point four, giving t about eight point three minutes.
The deeper point: the same twenty-degree drop takes longer the second time, because the block is now cooler and closer to the room, so a smaller excess means slower cooling.
हमारा advanced example Newton's cooling का मिज़ाज numbers में ही दिखा देता है।
एक metal block अस्सी से साठ degrees में, पाँच मिनट में ठंडा होता है, बीस के कमरे में। साठ से चालीस तक और ठंडा होने में कितना समय?
Average-temperature रूप use करो, हर interval में block का mean temperature लेते हुए।
पहला stage: eighty minus sixty बटा five बराबर k गुना average seventy, minus twenty। तो four बराबर fifty k, यानी k बराबर zero point zero eight per minute।
दूसरा stage वही k, अब mean temperature fifty: sixty minus forty बटा t बराबर zero point zero eight गुना thirty, यानी two point four।
तो twenty बटा t बराबर two point four, यानी t लगभग eight point three minutes।
गहरी बात: वही बीस-degree drop दूसरी बार ज़्यादा समय लेता है, क्योंकि block अब ठंडा है और कमरे के क़रीब, तो छोटा excess मतलब धीमी cooling।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for radiation

board_events.text: Traps in radiation and cooling
Using Celsius in Stefan's or Wien's law — both demand kelvin.
Dropping the surroundings term: net is eσA(T⁴ − T₀⁴), not eσAT⁴.
Emissive power (W per m sq) is not emissivity (a number 0 to 1).
Newton's cooling is for a small excess only; large gaps need full T⁴.
Pro-tip: for 'by what factor', use ratios in kelvin, skip the constants.
Mnemonics: power to the fourth in kelvin; hot is blue, cool is red.

segments.text: Let us close radiation with the traps that cost the most marks.
One: using Celsius in Stefan's or Wien's law. Both demand absolute kelvin, and with a fourth power a stray Celsius produces wildly wrong answers. Convert first, always.

Two: dropping the surroundings term. Net radiation is e sigma A times T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, not just e sigma A T to the fourth. A body in a warm room is also heated by the room.
Three: confusing emissive power with emissivity. Emissive power has units watts per square metre; emissivity is a dimensionless number between zero and one.
Four: applying Newton's cooling to large differences. It is an approximation for a small excess only; for a body far hotter than its surroundings, use the full Stefan fourth-power relation.

<whisper> The pro-tip: for any by-what-factor question, skip the constants entirely and use ratios in kelvin — power ratio is the temperature ratio to the fourth, and peak wavelength ratio is the inverse temperature ratio.
And the mnemonics: Stefan is power to the fourth, in kelvin; Wien says hot is blue, cool is red; and a black body absorbs all, emits all.
चलो radiation को उन traps के साथ ख़त्म करें जो सबसे ज़्यादा marks लेते हैं।
एक: Stefan's या Wien's law में Celsius use करना। दोनों absolute kelvin माँगते हैं, और चौथी power के साथ एक Celsius की भूल बेहद ग़लत answer देती है। पहले बदलो, हमेशा।
दो: surroundings term छोड़ना। Net radiation है e sigma A गुना T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, सिर्फ़ e sigma A T to the fourth नहीं। गरम कमरे में body को कमरा भी गरम करता है।
तीन: emissive power को emissivity से गड़बड़ाना। Emissive power की unit watts per square metre; emissivity zero और one के बीच एक dimensionless संख्या।
चार: Newton's cooling को बड़े फ़र्क़ पर लगाना। यह सिर्फ़ छोटे excess के लिए approximation है; surroundings से कहीं गरम body के लिए, पूरी Stefan fourth-power relation use करो।

<whisper> Pro-tip: किसी भी by-what-factor question के लिए, constants बिल्कुल छोड़ो और kelvin में ratios use करो — power ratio है temperature ratio का to the fourth, और peak wavelength ratio है उल्टा temperature ratio।
और mnemonics: Stefan है power to the fourth, kelvin में; Wien कहता है hot is blue, cool is red; और black body सब सोखता है, सब उगलता है।

segments.text: <curious> Part one told you what temperature is. Now the next question: how do we actually measure it?
You cannot read temperature directly — you read it through some property of a substance that changes reproducibly with hotness. That property is called a thermometric property.
A mercury-in-glass thermometer uses the length of a mercury column — as it warms, the mercury expands up the tube, and the length is your reading.

Different devices use different properties: a gas thermometer uses the pressure of a trapped gas, a platinum resistance thermometer uses electrical resistance, and a thermocouple uses a tiny thermo-e m f.
And a radiation pyrometer reads the radiation emitted by a very hot body — so it needs no contact at all, perfect for a furnace.
The same differential-expansion idea runs your geyser: a bimetallic strip, two metals with different alpha, bends as it heats.
As the strip bends it trips a switch, turning the heater off at the set temperature. A thermometer, in the end, is a translator from invisible hotness to a visible number.
<curious> Part one ने बताया temperature क्या है। अब अगला सवाल: हम इसे नापते असल में कैसे हैं?
Temperature सीधे नहीं पढ़ सकते — इसे किसी substance की उस property से पढ़ते हैं जो hotness के साथ दोबारा-दोबारा एक-सी बदलती है। उस property को thermometric property कहते हैं।
Mercury-in-glass thermometer, mercury column की length use करता है — गरम होने पर mercury tube में ऊपर चढ़ता है, और वो length ही आपकी reading।
अलग devices अलग properties use करते हैं: gas thermometer क़ैद gas का pressure, platinum resistance thermometer बिजली की resistance, और thermocouple एक छोटा thermo-e m f।
और radiation pyrometer किसी बहुत गरम body की निकलती radiation पढ़ता है — तो इसे contact की ज़रूरत ही नहीं, भट्टी के लिए बढ़िया।
यही differential-expansion idea आपका geyser चलाता है: एक bimetallic strip, अलग alpha वाले दो metals, गरम होने पर मुड़ जाती है।
जैसे strip मुड़ती है वो एक switch दबाती है, set temperature पर heater बंद कर देती है। Thermometer असल में एक translator है, अनदेखी hotness से दिखते number तक।

board_events.text: Dilute gases all agree — so the ideal-gas temperature is the standard.

segments.text: To turn a property into a number you need calibration: two reproducible fixed points.
The classic pair are the ice point — melting ice at one atmosphere, zero degrees — and the steam point — boiling water at one atmosphere, one hundred degrees.
Mark the property at both points, divide the span into one hundred equal parts, and you have a Celsius thermometer. So far, so neat.

But here is the subtlety. A mercury thermometer and an alcohol thermometer, both perfectly calibrated at zero and one hundred, disagree slightly at, say, fifty — because the two liquids do not expand in exactly the same non-linear way in between.
Which one tells the true temperature? Neither, exactly. That is what forced physicists to find a better standard.
The escape is the gas thermometer. Experiment shows that as you make a gas more and more dilute, all gases — hydrogen, helium, nitrogen — give the same reading.
That universality is why the ideal-gas temperature is adopted as the fundamental standard against which all other thermometers are checked.
किसी property को number बनाने के लिए calibration चाहिए: दो दोहराने योग्य fixed points।
Classic जोड़ी है ice point — one atmosphere पर पिघलती ice, zero degrees — और steam point — one atmosphere पर उबलता पानी, one hundred degrees।
दोनों points पर property mark करो, span को one hundred बराबर हिस्सों में बाँटो, और आपके पास Celsius thermometer है। यहाँ तक, सब साफ़।

पर यह रही बारीकी। एक mercury और एक alcohol thermometer, दोनों zero और one hundred पर perfectly calibrated, fifty पर थोड़ा अलग पढ़ते हैं — क्योंकि दोनों liquids बीच में बिल्कुल एक-सी non-linear way में नहीं फैलते।
कौन-सा सही temperature बताता है? कोई नहीं, ठीक-ठीक। यही वजह है कि physicists को बेहतर standard ढूँढना पड़ा।
बचाव है gas thermometer। Experiment दिखाता है कि gas को जितना dilute करो, सारी gases — hydrogen, helium, nitrogen — same reading देती हैं।
यही universality है जिससे ideal-gas temperature को बुनियादी standard माना जाता है, जिसके मुक़ाबले बाक़ी सारे thermometers जाँचे जाते हैं।

board_events.text: Each law holds a DIFFERENT variable fixed — do not mislabel which.
Together, in the ideal limit, they build the road to absolute temperature.

segments.text: Where does the absolute scale come from? It starts with three experimental gas laws, each for a fixed mass of gas in the ideal limit.
Boyle's law: at fixed temperature, pressure times volume is constant — squeeze the gas and the pressure rises.
In symbols, P V equals a constant, with the temperature held fixed.
Charles's law: at fixed pressure, volume is proportional to temperature — V over T is constant.
Gay-Lussac's law: at fixed volume, pressure is proportional to temperature — P over T is constant.
The key discipline: each law holds a different variable fixed — Boyle holds temperature, Charles holds pressure, Gay-Lussac holds volume. Mislabelling which is constant gives the wrong formula.
Together, in the dilute ideal limit, these three build the road that leads all the way to absolute temperature.
Absolute scale आता कहाँ से है? यह तीन experimental gas laws से शुरू होता है, हर एक fixed mass gas के लिए ideal limit में।
Boyle's law: fixed temperature पर, pressure गुना volume constant है — gas दबाओ तो pressure बढ़ता है।
Symbols में, P V बराबर एक constant, temperature fixed रखते हुए।
Charles's law: fixed pressure पर, volume, temperature के proportional है — V over T constant।
Gay-Lussac's law: fixed volume पर, pressure, temperature के proportional है — P over T constant।
मुख्य अनुशासन: हर law एक अलग variable fixed रखता है — Boyle temperature, Charles pressure, Gay-Lussac volume। कौन-सा constant है ग़लत बताना ग़लत formula देता है।
मिलकर, dilute ideal limit में, ये तीनों वो रास्ता बनाते हैं जो सीधे absolute temperature तक ले जाता है।

board_events.text: Plot P of a fixed-volume gas vs Celsius T: a straight line.
It crosses zero pressure at -273.15 C, for every gas.
The intercept is the same for every gas — a property of temperature itself.
Shift the origin here to define the Kelvin scale: P is proportional to T.
Combining the laws gives PV = nRT — valid at low pressure only.

segments.text: Now the beautiful step. Plot the pressure of a fixed-volume gas against Celsius temperature, and you get a straight line. What happens if we extend it backward?
Extrapolate that line backward, and it crosses zero pressure at minus two hundred seventy three point one five degrees Celsius.
And astonishingly, gases of every kind — hydrogen, helium, nitrogen — extrapolate to that same point.
A gas can have no less than zero pressure, so this common intercept is the coldest conceivable temperature: absolute zero.
Because the intercept is the same for every gas, it is a property of temperature itself, not of any particular gas.
Shift the origin to this point and you define the Kelvin scale, on which pressure — or volume — is simply proportional to temperature.

Combining the three laws gives the cleanest relationship in thermal physics, the ideal-gas equation P V equals n R T. Two cautions: it holds only at low pressure, and absolute zero can be approached, never reached.
अब ख़ूबसूरत क़दम। fixed-volume gas का pressure, Celsius temperature के मुक़ाबले plot करो, और सीधी line मिलती है। पीछे बढ़ाएँ तो क्या होता है?
उस line को पीछे extrapolate करो, और वो zero pressure को minus two hundred seventy three point one five degrees Celsius पर काटती है।
और हैरत की बात, हर तरह की gases — hydrogen, helium, nitrogen — उसी एक point पर extrapolate करती हैं।
किसी gas का pressure zero से कम नहीं हो सकता, तो यह common intercept सबसे ठंडा सोचने योग्य temperature है: absolute zero।
चूँकि intercept हर gas के लिए एक ही है, यह temperature की अपनी property है, किसी ख़ास gas की नहीं।
Origin को इस point पर shift करो और आप Kelvin scale define करते हैं, जिस पर pressure — या volume — सीधे temperature के proportional है।
तीनों laws मिलाकर thermal physics का सबसे साफ़ रिश्ता देते हैं, ideal-gas equation P V बराबर n R T। दो चेतावनियाँ: यह सिर्फ़ low pressure पर चलता है, और absolute zero को छुआ जा सकता है, पहुँचा नहीं।

sections.subtopic: Thermometry, the Ideal-Gas Equation and Absolute Temperature
sections.title: Thermometric relation, gas thermometer, absolute zero

board_events.text: Turning a property into a temperature
X is any thermometric property; X-naught and X-hundred its fixed-point values.
The gas thermometer needs only ONE fixed point: the triple point of water.
Absolute zero: an extrapolated limit, not an attainable state.

segments.text: Let us make the measurement formulas precise.
The linear thermometric relation: temperature t equals X at t minus X at zero, over X at one hundred minus X at zero, times one hundred degrees Celsius.
Here X is any thermometric property — a length, a pressure, a resistance — and its ice-point and steam-point values are X naught and X one hundred.
The constant-volume gas thermometer uses a single fixed point: T equals two seventy three point one six, times P over P at the triple point, in kelvin.
Notice it needs only one fixed point — the triple point of water — because, once pressure is proportional to temperature, a single reference fixes the whole scale.
And absolute zero: zero kelvin equals minus two seventy three point one five degrees Celsius.
Remember it is an extrapolated limit, not an attainable state — real systems get arbitrarily close but never reach it.
चलो measurement के formulas पक्के करें।
Linear thermometric relation: temperature t बराबर X at t minus X at zero, बटा X at one hundred minus X at zero, गुना one hundred degrees Celsius।
यहाँ X कोई भी thermometric property है — length, pressure, resistance — और ice-point व steam-point पर उसके values हैं X naught और X one hundred।
Constant-volume gas thermometer एक ही fixed point use करता है: T बराबर two seventy three point one six, गुना P बटा P triple point पर, kelvin में।
ध्यान दो इसे सिर्फ़ एक fixed point चाहिए — पानी का triple point — क्योंकि जब pressure, temperature के proportional हो, एक reference पूरी scale तय कर देता है।
और absolute zero: zero kelvin बराबर minus two seventy three point one five degrees Celsius।
याद रखो यह एक extrapolated हद है, पहुँचने योग्य हालत नहीं — असली systems बेहद क़रीब पहुँचते हैं पर कभी नहीं छूते।

sections.subtopic: Thermometry, the Ideal-Gas Equation and Absolute Temperature
sections.title: The gas laws combined and the ideal-gas equation

board_events.text: One identity for a fixed mass of gas
$R=8.314$ J per mol per K; $k_B=1.38\times10^{-23}$ J per K.
Triple point of water: 273.16 K at 611.7 Pa — this defines the kelvin.

segments.text: Now the combined toolkit for any fixed mass of gas.
The three laws again: Boyle, P V constant at fixed temperature; Charles, V over T constant at fixed pressure; Gay-Lussac, P over T constant at fixed volume.
Roll them into one identity between any two states: P one V one over T one equals P two V two over T two, with all temperatures in kelvin.
And the ideal-gas equation itself: P V equals n R T, which also equals capital N k B T.
The gas constant R is eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin, and the Boltzmann constant k B is one point three eight times ten to the minus twenty three joules per kelvin.

An ideal gas expands at constant pressure with coefficient one over two seventy three point one five, about three point six six times ten to the minus three per degree — far larger than any solid, and the same for all ideal gases.
And the triple point of water, two seventy three point one six kelvin at six hundred eleven point seven pascals, is the single state that defines the kelvin.
अब किसी fixed mass gas के लिए combined toolkit।
तीनों laws फिर: Boyle, fixed temperature पर P V constant; Charles, fixed pressure पर V over T constant; Gay-Lussac, fixed volume पर P over T constant।
इन्हें किन्हीं दो states के बीच एक identity में समेटो: P one V one बटा T one बराबर P two V two बटा T two, सारे temperatures kelvin में।
और ideal-gas equation ख़ुद: P V बराबर n R T, जो capital N k B T के भी बराबर।
Gas constant R है eight point three one four joules per mole per kelvin, और Boltzmann constant k B है one point three eight times ten to the minus twenty three joules per kelvin।

Ideal gas constant pressure पर coefficient one over two seventy three point one five से फैलती है, लगभग three point six six times ten to the minus three per degree — किसी भी solid से कहीं बड़ा, और सभी ideal gases के लिए एक-सा।
और पानी का triple point, two seventy three point one six kelvin, six hundred eleven point seven pascals पर, वो एक state है जो kelvin को define करता है।

sections.subtopic: Thermometry, the Ideal-Gas Equation and Absolute Temperature
sections.title: Deriving absolute zero from a gas thermometer

board_events.text: Absolute zero from a gas thermometer
Every dilute gas has the same gamma — a hint it is about temperature itself.
Same gamma for all gases means all extrapolate to the same intercept.
Adopt one reference, the triple point: $T=273.16\,P/P_{tr}$.

segments.text: Here is the board derivation: extrapolating a fixed-volume gas's pressure to zero defines a universal coldest temperature.

The experimental fact: for a fixed mass at fixed volume, the pressure varies linearly with Celsius temperature — P at t equals P naught times one plus gamma t, where gamma is one over two seventy three point one five.
Every dilute gas gives the same gamma, one over two seventy three point one five per degree — a strong hint that we are seeing a property of temperature, not of any gas.

A gas cannot push with negative pressure, so set P to zero: zero equals P naught times one plus t over two seventy three point one five, which gives t equals minus two seventy three point one five degrees Celsius.
Because gamma is the same for all gases, every gas extrapolates to this same intercept — the coldest conceivable temperature.
Now shift the origin: set T equals t plus two seventy three point one five. Then the relation collapses to P at t equals P naught times T over T naught — a pure proportionality, P proportional to T.

<excited> Once pressure is proportional to temperature, one reference suffices. Adopt the triple point at two seventy three point one six kelvin, and you recover the working formula, T equals two seventy three point one six times P over P at the triple point.
यह रहा board derivation: fixed-volume gas का pressure zero तक extrapolate करना एक universal सबसे ठंडा temperature define करता है।

Experimental सच: fixed mass, fixed volume पर, pressure, Celsius temperature के साथ linearly बदलता है — P at t बराबर P naught गुना one plus gamma t, जहाँ gamma है one over two seventy three point one five।
हर dilute gas वही gamma देती है, one over two seventy three point one five per degree — एक मज़बूत इशारा कि हम temperature की property देख रहे हैं, किसी gas की नहीं।

Gas negative pressure से धकेल नहीं सकती, तो P को zero रखो: zero बराबर P naught गुना one plus t बटा two seventy three point one five, जो देता है t बराबर minus two seventy three point one five degrees Celsius।
चूँकि gamma हर gas के लिए एक-सा है, हर gas इसी एक intercept पर extrapolate करती है — सबसे ठंडा सोचने योग्य temperature।
अब origin shift करो: T बराबर t plus two seventy three point one five रखो। तब relation सिमटकर बनता है P at t बराबर P naught गुना T over T naught — शुद्ध proportionality, P, T के proportional।

<excited> जब pressure, temperature के proportional हो, एक reference काफ़ी है। Triple point को two seventy three point one six kelvin पर अपनाओ, और working formula मिलता है, T बराबर two seventy three point one six गुना P बटा P triple point पर।

Since P is proportional to T, the temperature scales with the pressure ratio.
One fixed point suffices once P is proportional to T — a neat economy.

segments.text: A clean board reading of a constant-volume gas thermometer.
The thermometer reads a pressure of eighty millimetres of mercury when its bulb sits at the triple point of water. Placed in a hot bath, the pressure rises to one hundred. Find the bath temperature.
So the triple-point pressure is eighty, and the bath pressure is one hundred.
Because pressure is proportional to absolute temperature, the temperature scales directly with the pressure ratio.
So T equals two seventy three point one six, times one hundred over eighty — which is three hundred forty one point four five kelvin.
In Celsius, that is about sixty eight point three degrees.
Notice the economy: the gas thermometer needs only one fixed point, the triple point, because once pressure is proportional to temperature a single reference fixes the whole scale.
Constant-volume gas thermometer की एक साफ़ board reading।
Thermometer eighty millimetres of mercury का pressure पढ़ता है जब उसका bulb पानी के triple point पर हो। गरम bath में रखने पर pressure one hundred तक बढ़ता है। Bath का temperature निकालो।
तो triple-point pressure है eighty, और bath pressure है one hundred।
चूँकि pressure, absolute temperature के proportional है, temperature सीधे pressure ratio के साथ scale होता है।
तो T बराबर two seventy three point one six, गुना one hundred over eighty — यानी three hundred forty one point four five kelvin।
Celsius में, यह लगभग sixty eight point three degrees।
Economy देखो: gas thermometer को सिर्फ़ एक fixed point चाहिए, triple point, क्योंकि जब pressure, temperature के proportional हो एक reference पूरी scale तय कर देता है।

board_events.text: Trap: 'volume doubles, so double 27 to 54 C.' Charles's law uses kelvin.
Convert to kelvin before any ratio.
Doubling the Celsius reading is the deadliest trap — the offset wrecks it.

segments.text: The most common NEET gas-law trap, and it is all about units.
A fixed mass of gas at twenty seven degrees Celsius is heated at constant pressure until its volume doubles. Find the final temperature.
The reflex is: volume doubles, so double twenty seven to fifty four degrees. That is wrong — Charles's law is volume proportional to temperature, with temperature in kelvin, never Celsius.
Convert first: twenty seven degrees Celsius is three hundred kelvin.

Then volume proportional to temperature means doubling the volume doubles the absolute temperature: T two equals two times three hundred, six hundred kelvin, which is three hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius.
The rule for every gas-law problem: convert to kelvin before taking any ratio.
Doubling the Celsius reading is the single most common error, because the two seventy three offset quietly wrecks the proportion.
सबसे आम NEET gas-law trap, और यह पूरी तरह units की बात है।
Twenty seven degrees Celsius पर एक fixed mass gas को constant pressure पर गरम किया जाता है जब तक volume दुगना न हो। Final temperature निकालो।
Reflex है: volume दुगना, तो twenty seven को दुगना करके fifty four degrees। यह ग़लत है — Charles's law है volume, temperature के proportional, temperature kelvin में, Celsius में कभी नहीं।
पहले बदलो: twenty seven degrees Celsius है three hundred kelvin।
फिर volume, temperature के proportional मतलब volume दुगना करने पर absolute temperature दुगना: T two बराबर two गुना three hundred, six hundred kelvin, यानी three hundred twenty seven degrees Celsius।
हर gas-law problem का rule: कोई भी ratio लेने से पहले kelvin में बदलो।
Celsius reading दुगना करना सबसे आम ग़लती है, क्योंकि two seventy three offset चुपचाप proportion बिगाड़ देता है।

segments.text: Now a constant-volume problem — a sealed rigid vessel.
A sealed rigid vessel contains gas at twenty seven degrees Celsius and one atmosphere. It is heated to one hundred twenty seven. Find the new pressure.
The vessel is rigid, so the volume is constant — this is Gay-Lussac's law, pressure proportional to temperature.
Work in kelvin: twenty seven degrees is three hundred, one hundred twenty seven is four hundred.
So P two equals P one times T two over T one: one atmosphere times four hundred over three hundred, which is four thirds, about one point three three atmospheres.
Notice a hundred-degree rise sounds large but is only a thirty three percent pressure increase, because on the absolute scale three hundred to four hundred is a factor of four thirds.
Reason in kelvin, always: the Celsius reading, twenty seven to one hundred twenty seven, misleadingly suggests a factor of about five.
अब एक constant-volume problem — एक sealed rigid vessel।
एक sealed rigid vessel में gas है twenty seven degrees Celsius और one atmosphere पर। इसे one hundred twenty seven तक गरम किया जाता है। नया pressure निकालो।
Vessel कड़ा है, तो volume constant — यह Gay-Lussac's law है, pressure, temperature के proportional।
Kelvin में काम करो: twenty seven degrees है three hundred, one hundred twenty seven है four hundred।
तो P two बराबर P one गुना T two over T one: one atmosphere गुना four hundred over three hundred, यानी four thirds, लगभग one point three three atmospheres।
ध्यान दो सौ-degree rise बड़ा लगता है पर बस thirty three percent pressure बढ़ोतरी है, क्योंकि absolute scale पर three hundred से four hundred, four thirds का factor है।
हमेशा kelvin में सोचो: Celsius reading, twenty seven से one hundred twenty seven, धोखे से लगभग पाँच का factor दिखाती है।

Absolute zero recovered from nothing but two pressure readings.
The ratio 1.366 = 373.15/273.15 is the absolute scale inside Celsius data.

segments.text: Our advanced example recovers absolute zero from just two measurements.

In a constant-volume gas thermometer the pressure is one point zero zero zero atmosphere at the ice point, zero degrees, and one point three six six at the steam point, one hundred degrees. Treating pressure as linear in Celsius, find the absolute zero the data implies.
Model the pressure as P equals a plus b t, with t in degrees Celsius.

At t equals zero, P is one, so a is one point zero zero zero. The slope b is one point three six six minus one, over one hundred — three point six six times ten to the minus three atmospheres per degree.
Now set P to zero: zero equals a plus b t naught, so t naught equals minus a over b — about minus two seventy three point two degrees Celsius.
Absolute zero, recovered from nothing but two pressure readings — exactly how it was first pinned down, not by reaching it, but by extrapolating a straight line to zero pressure.
And the fingerprint is right there: the ratio one point three six six equals three seventy three point one five over two seventy three point one five — the absolute scale hiding inside Celsius data.
हमारा advanced example सिर्फ़ दो measurements से absolute zero निकाल लेता है।

एक constant-volume gas thermometer में pressure है one point zero zero zero atmosphere ice point पर, zero degrees, और one point three six six steam point पर, one hundred degrees। Pressure को Celsius में linear मानकर, data जो absolute zero बताता है निकालो।
Pressure को P बराबर a plus b t model करो, t degrees Celsius में।
t बराबर zero पर, P है one, तो a है one point zero zero zero। Slope b है one point three six six minus one, बटा one hundred — three point six six times ten to the minus three atmospheres per degree।
अब P को zero रखो: zero बराबर a plus b t naught, तो t naught बराबर minus a over b — लगभग minus two seventy three point two degrees Celsius।
Absolute zero, सिर्फ़ दो pressure readings से निकाला — ठीक वैसे जैसे पहली बार पता चला, इसे पहुँचकर नहीं, बल्कि एक सीधी line को zero pressure तक extrapolate करके।
और fingerprint वहीं है: ratio one point three six six बराबर three seventy three point one five बटा two seventy three point one five — Celsius data के अंदर छिपी absolute scale।

board_events.text: Traps in thermometry and gas laws
Using Celsius in a gas law — all gas laws need kelvin.
Absolute zero is an extrapolated limit — approached, never reached.
Confusing the three laws: hold the right variable fixed.
Triple point (273.16 K) is not the ordinary ice point (273.15 K at 1 atm).
Using a thermometer outside its range gives nonsense.
Pro-tip: combine the laws as P1V1/T1 = P2V2/T2, kelvin throughout.

segments.text: Let us close thermometry with its traps.

One, the deadliest: using Celsius in a gas law. Pressure proportional to temperature, volume proportional to temperature, and P V equals n R T all require kelvin. Convert before forming any ratio — the two seventy three offset is fatal.
Two: thinking absolute zero is attainable. It is an extrapolated limit; real systems get arbitrarily close but never reach zero kelvin.
Three: confusing the three gas laws. Hold the right variable fixed — Boyle temperature, Charles pressure, Gay-Lussac volume. Mislabelling which is constant gives a wrong formula.

Four: mixing up the triple point and the ice point. The triple point is two seventy three point one six kelvin at low pressure, with three phases coexisting — not the ordinary ice point at one atmosphere. They differ by a hundredth of a kelvin, but the triple point is the defining fixed point.
Five: using a thermometer outside its range gives nonsense — mercury freezes at minus thirty nine degrees, so pick the device whose substance spans the range you need.

<whisper> The pro-tip: never memorise three separate laws — combine them as P one V one over T one equals P two V two over T two, in kelvin throughout. Every gas problem is that one identity with one quantity held fixed.
चलो thermometry को उसके traps के साथ ख़त्म करें।

एक, सबसे ख़तरनाक: gas law में Celsius use करना। Pressure proportional to temperature, volume proportional to temperature, और P V बराबर n R T सब kelvin माँगते हैं। कोई भी ratio बनाने से पहले बदलो — two seventy three offset जानलेवा है।
दो: सोचना कि absolute zero पहुँचने योग्य है। यह एक extrapolated हद है; असली systems बेहद क़रीब पहुँचते हैं पर zero kelvin कभी नहीं छूते।
तीन: तीनों gas laws में गड़बड़। सही variable fixed रखो — Boyle temperature, Charles pressure, Gay-Lussac volume। कौन-सा constant है ग़लत बताना ग़लत formula देता है।

चार: triple point और ice point में उलझना। Triple point है two seventy three point one six kelvin, low pressure पर, तीन phases साथ — न कि one atmosphere पर साधारण ice point। ये सौवें kelvin से अलग हैं, पर triple point ही defining fixed point है।
पाँच: thermometer को उसकी range से बाहर use करना बकवास देता है — mercury minus thirty nine degrees पर जम जाता है, तो वो device चुनो जिसका substance ज़रूरी range cover करे।
<whisper> Pro-tip: तीन अलग laws कभी मत रटो — इन्हें P one V one बटा T one बराबर P two V two बटा T two की तरह combine करो, पूरे में kelvin। हर gas problem वही एक identity है, एक quantity fixed रखकर।

Sublimation: solid straight to gas — dry ice, camphor, naphthalene, iodine.
Each transition happens at a fixed temperature for a given pressure.
Latent heat flows in or out during every transition (Q = mL).
Part two counted this heat; here we ask WHEN and WHY states change.

segments.text: <curious> In part two you learned to count the heat a phase change costs. But when and why a substance changes state — and how pressure shifts it — is a separate, heavily tested story.
Matter exists in three common states, and a pure substance moves between them along three borders.
Melting and freezing between solid and liquid; vaporization and condensation between liquid and gas.
And the third: sublimation, solid straight to gas with no liquid in between — dry ice, camphor, naphthalene balls, iodine.
Each transition, for a pure substance, happens at a fixed temperature for a given pressure.
And during every transition, latent heat flows in or out — the same Q equals m L you already know.
In part two you counted that heat and budgeted it. Here the question is different: when, and why, does a state change happen at all?
<curious> Part two में आपने phase change की heat गिनना सीखा। पर कोई substance state बदलता कब और क्यों है — और pressure इसे कैसे खिसकाता है — यह एक अलग, ख़ूब पूछा जाने वाला किस्सा है।
पदार्थ तीन आम states में रहता है, और एक pure substance इनके बीच तीन borders पर चलता है।
Melting और freezing, solid और liquid के बीच; vaporization और condensation, liquid और gas के बीच।
और तीसरा: sublimation, solid सीधे gas में, बीच में कोई liquid नहीं — dry ice, camphor, naphthalene की गोलियाँ, iodine।
हर transition, pure substance के लिए, दिए pressure पर एक fixed temperature पर होता है।
और हर transition के दौरान, latent heat अंदर या बाहर बहती है — वही Q बराबर m L जो आप जानते हैं।
Part two में आपने वो heat गिनी और budget की। यहाँ सवाल अलग है: state change होता कब, और क्यों है?

board_events.text: Pressure moves the transition temperatures
Most substances: melting point RISES with pressure (dense solid is favoured).
Water rebels: ice is less dense, so its melting point FALLS with pressure.

board_events.text: Regelation: pressure under a wire melts ice; it refreezes once pressure lifts.
Boiling: a liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the external pressure.
Higher external pressure raises the boiling point; lower pressure lowers it.

segments.text: Now the heavily tested part: how pressure shifts these transition temperatures.
For most substances the melting point rises as pressure increases — squeezing favours the denser solid.
Water is the famous rebel. Ice is less dense than liquid water — it expands on freezing, which is why pipes burst — so for water the melting point falls with pressure.
This single fact powers regelation: press a fine wire over an ice block, and the high pressure under the wire lowers the local melting point.
The ice melts, the wire sinks through, and the water refreezes above it once the pressure is gone — leaving the block whole. It is also the textbook story of why ice is slippery under a skate.
Now boiling. A liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the external pressure pressing down on it.
So raise the external pressure and you need a higher temperature to boil — the pressure cooker. Lower it, high in the mountains, and water boils below one hundred degrees, so food cooks slowly.
अब ख़ूब पूछा जाने वाला हिस्सा: pressure इन transition temperatures को कैसे खिसकाता है।
ज़्यादातर substances के लिए melting point pressure बढ़ने पर बढ़ता है — दबाव denser solid को पसंद करता है।
पानी मशहूर बाग़ी है। Ice, liquid पानी से कम dense है — यह जमने पर फैलता है, इसीलिए pipes फटती हैं — तो पानी का melting point pressure के साथ गिरता है।
यही एक बात regelation चलाती है: ice block पर एक बारीक wire दबाओ, और wire के नीचे का high pressure वहाँ का melting point गिरा देता है।
Ice पिघलती है, wire नीचे धँसती है, और pressure हटते ही पानी उसके ऊपर फिर जम जाता है — block पूरा छोड़कर। यही skate के नीचे ice की फिसलन का textbook किस्सा भी है।
अब boiling। एक liquid तब उबलता है जब उसका saturated vapour pressure, उस पर दबते external pressure के बराबर हो जाए।
तो external pressure बढ़ाओ और उबलने के लिए ज़्यादा temperature चाहिए — pressure cooker। इसे घटाओ, ऊँचे पहाड़ों में, और पानी one hundred degrees से नीचे उबलता है, तो खाना धीरे पकता है।

board_events.text: Three regions (solid, liquid, gas), three curves (fusion, vaporization, sublimation).
The triple point: the one P and T where all three phases coexist.
Water's triple point: 273.16 K at 611.7 Pa — it also anchors the kelvin.
The vaporization curve ends at the critical point (water: 647 K, 22.1 MPa).
Above the critical temperature, no pressure can liquefy the gas.

segments.text: Plot pressure against temperature and you get a phase diagram — a map of which state a substance prefers at each pressure and temperature.
Three regions — solid, liquid, gas — separated by three curves: the fusion curve, the vaporization curve, and the sublimation curve. Cross a curve and the substance switches state.
Each curve is a two-phase equilibrium — along it, the substance can sit as either phase, or a mix.
All three curves meet at one special point — the triple point — the only pressure and temperature at which solid, liquid and vapour coexist in equilibrium.
For water, that is two seventy three point one six kelvin at six hundred eleven point seven pascals — a fixed, reproducible state, which is exactly why it anchors the kelvin.
The vaporization curve does not go on forever — it ends at the critical point. For water, six hundred forty seven kelvin and twenty two point one megapascals.
Above the critical temperature there is no liquid-gas distinction at all — you cannot liquefy a gas by pressure alone, no matter how hard you squeeze.
Pressure को temperature के मुक़ाबले plot करो और phase diagram मिलता है — एक नक़्शा कि हर pressure और temperature पर substance कौन-सा state पसंद करता है।
तीन regions — solid, liquid, gas — तीन curves से अलग: fusion curve, vaporization curve, और sublimation curve। एक curve पार करो और substance state बदल देता है।
हर curve एक two-phase equilibrium है — उस पर substance किसी भी phase में, या mix में रह सकता है।
तीनों curves एक ख़ास point पर मिलती हैं — triple point — वो अकेला pressure और temperature जहाँ solid, liquid और vapour एक साथ equilibrium में रहते हैं।
पानी के लिए, यह है two seventy three point one six kelvin, six hundred eleven point seven pascals पर — एक fixed, दोहराने योग्य state, इसीलिए यह kelvin को anchor करता है।
Vaporization curve हमेशा नहीं चलती — यह critical point पर ख़त्म होती है। पानी के लिए, six hundred forty seven kelvin और twenty two point one megapascals।
Critical temperature के ऊपर liquid-gas का फ़र्क़ ही नहीं रहता — आप सिर्फ़ pressure से gas को liquid नहीं कर सकते, चाहे कितना भी दबाओ।

board_events.text: Boiling: a bulk phenomenon at the boiling point — bubbles throughout.
Evaporation: only at the surface, at any temperature — the fastest escape.
So evaporation cools: sweat, the earthen matka, the desert cooler.
It speeds up with higher temperature, more surface, drier air, and wind.
Phase diagrams assume a pure substance; impurities shift the points.

segments.text: One more distinction, and it is a favourite conceptual trap: evaporation is not boiling.
Boiling is a bulk phenomenon at the boiling point — bubbles form throughout the liquid. Evaporation happens only at the surface, and at any temperature.
In evaporation, the fastest surface molecules escape, leaving the rest cooler.
That is why evaporation cools. Sweat evaporating cools your skin; water seeping through a porous earthen pot, a matka, keeps the water inside cool.
A desert cooler works the same way — evaporating water into dry air.
Evaporation speeds up with higher temperature, a larger surface area, drier air with low humidity, and moving air — wind.

And one caution: phase diagrams and fixed transition temperatures apply to pure substances. Impurities and dissolved solutes shift them — salt lowers ice's melting point, dissolved solids raise the boiling point.
एक और फ़र्क़, और यह पसंदीदा conceptual trap है: evaporation, boiling नहीं है।
Boiling एक bulk phenomenon है boiling point पर — पूरे liquid में bubbles बनते हैं। Evaporation सिर्फ़ सतह पर होता है, और किसी भी temperature पर।
Evaporation में, सबसे तेज़ सतह वाले molecules भाग जाते हैं, बाक़ी को ठंडा छोड़कर।
इसीलिए evaporation ठंडक देता है। पसीना evaporate होकर skin ठंडी करता है; झरझरे मिट्टी के मटके से रिसता पानी अंदर के पानी को ठंडा रखता है।
Desert cooler भी वैसे ही चलता है — सूखी हवा में पानी evaporate करके।
Evaporation तेज़ होता है ज़्यादा temperature, बड़े surface area, कम humidity वाली सूखी हवा, और चलती हवा — wind से।

और एक चेतावनी: phase diagrams और fixed transition temperatures pure substances के लिए हैं। Impurities और घुले solutes इन्हें खिसकाते हैं — नमक ice का melting point गिराता है, घुले solids boiling point बढ़ाते हैं।

sections.title: The change-of-state facts and constants

board_events.text: Change-of-state facts to carry
Melting point vs pressure: water decreases (~ minus 0.0075 C/atm); most increase.
Boiling point vs pressure: rises with pressure; falls at altitude.
Sublimation occurs when the ambient pressure is below the triple-point pressure.

segments.text: Let us gather the change-of-state facts worth carrying into the exam.
The latent-heat relation, from part two: Q equals m L, with fusion eighty calories per gram and vaporization five hundred forty.
Melting point versus pressure: for water it decreases, about minus zero point zero zero seven five degrees per atmosphere; for most substances it increases.
Boiling point versus pressure: it rises with external pressure — the pressure cooker — and falls at high altitude, giving slow mountain cooking.
The triple point of water: two seventy three point one six kelvin at six hundred eleven point seven pascals.
And the critical point of water: six hundred forty seven kelvin at twenty two point one megapascals, above which no pressure can liquefy the gas.
And a clean rule for sublimation: it occurs when the ambient pressure is below the substance's triple-point pressure — which is why dry ice sublimes at one atmosphere.
चलो change-of-state के वो facts इकट्ठा करें जो exam में ले जाने लायक हैं।
Part two से latent-heat relation: Q बराबर m L, fusion eighty calories per gram और vaporization five hundred forty।
Melting point बनाम pressure: पानी के लिए घटता है, लगभग minus zero point zero zero seven five degrees per atmosphere; ज़्यादातर substances के लिए बढ़ता है।
Boiling point बनाम pressure: external pressure के साथ बढ़ता है — pressure cooker — और ऊँचाई पर गिरता है, धीमी mountain cooking देता है।
पानी का triple point: two seventy three point one six kelvin, six hundred eleven point seven pascals पर।
और पानी का critical point: six hundred forty seven kelvin, twenty two point one megapascals पर, जिसके ऊपर कोई pressure gas को liquid नहीं कर सकता।
और sublimation का साफ़ rule: यह तब होता है जब ambient pressure, substance के triple-point pressure से नीचे हो — इसीलिए dry ice one atmosphere पर sublime करता है।

board_events.text: The sign of the fusion curve

Water: ice to water shrinks, so the volume change is negative and the slope is negative.

board_events.text: So one sign separates water from a normal substance.
You rarely compute it — read its sign, and the behaviour falls out.

segments.text: The deepest idea in this subtopic is a single sign, from the Clausius-Clapeyron relation.
It says d P by d T along a phase boundary equals L over T times delta V, where delta V is the volume change in the transition.
Computing with it is beyond the core syllabus, but the sign of delta V is the whole insight.

For water's fusion, ice turning to water shrinks — the volume change is negative — so d P by d T is negative. The fusion line slopes backward, which is exactly why water's melting point falls with pressure.
Compare a normal substance: its solid is denser than its liquid, so the volume change is positive, the slope is positive, and its melting point rises with pressure.
So the whole difference between water and a normal substance — regelation or no regelation — comes from one sign.
You do not need to compute Clausius-Clapeyron in most problems. Read its sign, and the everyday behaviour falls out.
इस subtopic का सबसे गहरा idea एक अकेला sign है, Clausius-Clapeyron relation से।
यह कहता है phase boundary पर d P by d T बराबर L over T गुना delta V, जहाँ delta V transition में volume change है।
इससे हिसाब करना core syllabus से बाहर है, पर delta V का sign ही पूरी समझ है।
पानी के fusion के लिए, ice से पानी बनने पर सिकुड़ता है — volume change negative — तो d P by d T negative। Fusion line पीछे झुकती है, यही वजह है कि पानी का melting point pressure से गिरता है।
एक normal substance से तुलना करो: इसका solid, liquid से denser है, तो volume change positive, slope positive, और इसका melting point pressure से बढ़ता है।
तो पानी और normal substance के बीच का सारा फ़र्क़ — regelation या नहीं — एक sign से आता है।
ज़्यादातर problems में Clausius-Clapeyron compute करने की ज़रूरत नहीं। इसका sign पढ़ो, और रोज़मर्रा का behaviour निकल आता है।

board_events.text: A liquid boils when its vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure.
Cooker: trapped steam raises pressure, so water boils above 100 C — faster.
Hill station: low air pressure, so water boils below 100 C — slower.
The controlling variable is always the temperature of the boiling water.
Higher pressure means higher boiling point means faster cooking.

segments.text: A classic board explain-with-reason question.
Explain, using boiling point and pressure, why food cooks faster in a pressure cooker than in an open pan, and slower at a high-altitude hill station.
Start from the principle: a liquid boils when its saturated vapour pressure equals the surrounding pressure.

In a pressure cooker the trapped steam raises the internal pressure well above one atmosphere, so the boiling point of water climbs above one hundred degrees. Food sits in hotter water and cooks faster.
At a hill station the atmospheric pressure is lower, so water boils below one hundred degrees. The cooler boiling water transfers heat more slowly, and cooking takes longer.
The controlling variable is always the temperature of the boiling water, and that temperature is set by the pressure.
Higher pressure means a higher boiling point means faster cooking — that is the whole chain.
एक classic board explain-with-reason सवाल।
Boiling point और pressure से समझाओ कि pressure cooker में खाना खुले pan से तेज़ क्यों पकता है, और ऊँचे hill station पर धीमा क्यों।
सिद्धांत से शुरू: एक liquid तब उबलता है जब उसका saturated vapour pressure, चारों ओर के pressure के बराबर हो।
Pressure cooker में क़ैद steam अंदर का pressure one atmosphere से ख़ासा ऊपर उठाता है, तो पानी का boiling point one hundred degrees के ऊपर चढ़ता है। खाना ज़्यादा गरम पानी में बैठकर तेज़ पकता है।
Hill station पर atmospheric pressure कम होता है, तो पानी one hundred degrees से नीचे उबलता है। ठंडा उबलता पानी heat धीरे देता है, और पकने में ज़्यादा समय लगता है।
Controlling variable हमेशा उबलते पानी का temperature है, और वो temperature pressure से तय होता है।
ज़्यादा pressure मतलब ज़्यादा boiling point मतलब तेज़ पकना — यही पूरी chain है।

board_events.text: Trap: 'the wire cut through.' It did not — the ice melted and refroze.
High pressure under the wire lowers the melting point; the ice melts.
Above the wire, pressure released, the water refreezes — releasing latent heat.
The wire descends and the block re-fuses behind it, staying whole.
This is regelation — it works only because ice's melting point falls with pressure.

segments.text: A NEET favourite that punishes the obvious answer.

A copper wire carrying heavy weights at both ends is hung over a slab of ice. After some time the wire has passed completely through it, yet the slab remains a single solid block. Name and explain the phenomenon.
The trap is to say the wire cut or sawed through the ice. It did not cut — the ice melted and refroze.
The large pressure directly beneath the wire lowers the melting point of the ice there, because water's melting point falls with pressure. So the ice melts under the wire and lets it sink.

Above the wire, where the pressure is released, the water is below the normal melting point again, so it refreezes — and that releases its latent heat, which supplies the heat to melt the ice just ahead.
So the wire descends through the block, which re-fuses behind it and stays whole.
This is regelation. It works only because ice's melting point falls with pressure — a substance whose melting point rises would not let the wire through.
एक NEET पसंदीदा जो obvious answer की सज़ा देता है।
एक copper wire, दोनों सिरों पर भारी weights के साथ, ice के slab पर लटकाई जाती है। कुछ देर बाद wire इसके आर-पार निकल जाती है, फिर भी slab एक ही solid block रहता है। Phenomenon का नाम और वजह बताओ।
Trap है यह कहना कि wire ने ice को काटा। इसने काटा नहीं — ice पिघली और फिर जमी।
Wire के ठीक नीचे का बड़ा pressure वहाँ ice का melting point गिराता है, क्योंकि पानी का melting point pressure से गिरता है। तो wire के नीचे ice पिघलती है और उसे धँसने देती है।
Wire के ऊपर, जहाँ pressure हट जाता है, पानी फिर normal melting point से नीचे है, तो वो फिर जम जाता है — और वो अपनी latent heat छोड़ता है, जो ठीक आगे की ice पिघलाने की heat देता है।
तो wire block के आर-पार उतरती है, जो पीछे फिर जुड़कर पूरा रहता है।
यह regelation है। यह सिर्फ़ इसलिए चलता है क्योंकि ice का melting point pressure से गिरता है — जिस substance का melting point बढ़ता हो वो wire को निकलने न दे।

board_events.text: CO2 triple point: 216.6 K at 5.1 atm — well above 1 atm.
A liquid phase exists only above the triple-point pressure.
At 1 atm, below 5.1 atm, the line crosses only the sublimation curve.
A substance sublimes at any ambient pressure below its triple-point pressure.

segments.text: A phase-diagram argument, and a satisfying one.

Solid carbon dioxide, dry ice, has a triple point at two hundred sixteen point six kelvin and five point one atmospheres. Explain why, at ordinary one atmosphere, it turns directly into gas without ever becoming a liquid.
On the carbon dioxide phase diagram, the triple point sits at five point one atmospheres — well above one atmosphere.
And a liquid phase exists only at pressures above the triple-point pressure — the liquid region lies above the triple point.
So at one atmosphere, a horizontal line lies below the triple point. As the solid warms it crosses only the sublimation curve, never entering the liquid region.
Hence dry ice goes straight from solid to vapour — it sublimes. To get liquid carbon dioxide you must first raise the pressure above five point one atmospheres.

The rule generalises: a substance sublimes at any ambient pressure below its triple-point pressure. Water's triple-point pressure is far below one atmosphere, which is why water melts rather than sublimes.
एक phase-diagram तर्क, और एक संतोषजनक वाला।

Solid carbon dioxide, dry ice, का triple point है two hundred sixteen point six kelvin और five point one atmospheres पर। समझाओ कि साधारण one atmosphere पर यह सीधे gas में क्यों बदलता है, कभी liquid बने बिना।
Carbon dioxide phase diagram पर, triple point five point one atmospheres पर बैठता है — one atmosphere से ख़ासा ऊपर।
और liquid phase सिर्फ़ triple-point pressure के ऊपर के pressures पर होता है — liquid region triple point के ऊपर है।
तो one atmosphere पर, एक horizontal line triple point के नीचे रहती है। जैसे solid गरम होता है वो सिर्फ़ sublimation curve पार करता है, liquid region में घुसता ही नहीं।
इसलिए dry ice सीधे solid से vapour जाता है — sublime करता है। Liquid carbon dioxide पाने के लिए पहले pressure को five point one atmospheres के ऊपर करना होगा।

Rule generalize होता है: कोई substance अपने triple-point pressure से नीचे किसी भी ambient pressure पर sublime करता है। पानी का triple-point pressure one atmosphere से बहुत नीचे है, इसीलिए पानी sublime के बजाय melt करता है।

board_events.text: So the melting point falls by about 0.0074 C per atmosphere.
The negative sign traces straight to ice being less dense than water.

segments.text: Our advanced example puts a number on water's most famous anomaly.
Estimate the change in the melting point of ice when the pressure is increased by one atmosphere, using the Clausius-Clapeyron relation.

First the volume change per kilogram on melting: one over the density of water minus one over the density of ice, which is minus nine point zero five times ten to the minus five cubic metres per kilogram — negative, because water is denser than ice.
Invert Clausius-Clapeyron for d T by d P: temperature times delta V over L, about minus seven point three five times ten to the minus eight kelvin per pascal.
Multiply by one atmosphere, one point zero one three times ten to the five pascals: delta T is about minus seven point four times ten to the minus three kelvin.
So the melting point falls by about zero point zero zero seven four degrees per atmosphere — a tiny but real drop.

<excited> The negative sign is the entire point — it traces straight to the volume change being negative, the fact that ice is less dense than water. For a normal substance the same relation gives a melting point that rises with pressure.
हमारा advanced example पानी की सबसे मशहूर anomaly पर एक number रखता है।
Clausius-Clapeyron relation से अंदाज़ा लगाओ कि pressure one atmosphere बढ़ाने पर ice का melting point कितना बदलता है।

पहले melting पर per kilogram volume change: one over पानी की density minus one over ice की density, यानी minus nine point zero five times ten to the minus five cubic metres per kilogram — negative, क्योंकि पानी, ice से denser है।
Clausius-Clapeyron को d T by d P के लिए उल्टो: temperature गुना delta V बटा L, लगभग minus seven point three five times ten to the minus eight kelvin per pascal।
One atmosphere से गुणा करो, one point zero one three times ten to the five pascals: delta T लगभग minus seven point four times ten to the minus three kelvin।
तो melting point लगभग zero point zero zero seven four degrees per atmosphere गिरता है — छोटा पर असली drop।

<excited> Negative sign ही सब कुछ है — यह सीधे volume change के negative होने से आता है, इस बात से कि ice पानी से कम dense है। Normal substance के लिए वही relation pressure से बढ़ता melting point देता है।

sections.title: Pitfalls and pro-tips for change of state

board_events.text: Traps in change of state
Not every melting point rises with pressure — water is the exception.
Regelation is not cutting — the ice melts under pressure and refreezes.
The triple point is a single P and T, not the 1-atm melting or boiling point.
A gas above its critical temperature cannot be liquefied by any pressure.
Evaporation: surface, any temperature, cools. Boiling: bulk, at the boiling point.
Pro-tip: solve conceptual questions on the phase map — slide along a P or T line.

segments.text: Let us close change of state, and the whole chapter's teaching, with its traps.

One: assuming every melting point rises with pressure. Water is the great exception — its solid is less dense than its liquid, so its melting point falls. Check which is denser before guessing the sign.
Two: calling regelation cutting. The wire never cuts the ice — the ice melts under pressure and refreezes when the pressure is released. The block stays whole.

Three: confusing the triple point with the ice or boiling point. The triple point is a single pressure and temperature, at low pressure, with three phases coexisting — not the ordinary one-atmosphere melting or boiling point.
Four: thinking a gas can always be liquefied by pressure. Above the critical temperature, no amount of pressure produces a liquid — the liquid-gas border simply ends at the critical point.
Five: mixing up evaporation and boiling. Evaporation is a surface phenomenon at any temperature that cools the liquid; boiling is a bulk phenomenon at the boiling point that needs continuous heat.

<whisper> The pro-tip: solve every conceptual question on the phase map. Sketch a quick pressure-temperature diagram, mark the triple and critical points, and slide along a constant-pressure or constant-temperature line to see which border you cross — pressure cooker, mountain cooking, dry ice, regelation, all fall out of that one picture.
चलो change of state, और पूरे chapter की teaching, को उसके traps के साथ ख़त्म करें।
एक: मानना कि हर melting point pressure से बढ़ता है। पानी बड़ा अपवाद है — इसका solid, liquid से कम dense है, तो इसका melting point गिरता है। Sign अंदाज़ने से पहले देखो कौन denser है।
दो: regelation को cutting कहना। Wire ice को कभी नहीं काटती — ice pressure में पिघलती है और pressure हटने पर फिर जमती है। Block पूरा रहता है।
तीन: triple point को ice या boiling point से गड़बड़ाना। Triple point एक अकेला pressure और temperature है, low pressure पर, तीन phases के साथ — न कि साधारण one-atmosphere melting या boiling point।
चार: सोचना कि gas हमेशा pressure से liquid हो सकती है। Critical temperature के ऊपर, कितना भी pressure liquid नहीं बनाता — liquid-gas border critical point पर ख़त्म हो जाता है।
पाँच: evaporation और boiling में उलझना। Evaporation किसी भी temperature पर एक surface phenomenon है जो liquid ठंडा करता है; boiling, boiling point पर एक bulk phenomenon है जिसे लगातार heat चाहिए।

<whisper> Pro-tip: हर conceptual सवाल phase map पर हल करो। एक झटपट pressure-temperature diagram बनाओ, triple और critical points mark करो, और constant-pressure या constant-temperature line पर सरको यह देखने को कि कौन-सा border पार करते हो — pressure cooker, mountain cooking, dry ice, regelation, सब उसी एक तस्वीर से निकलते हैं।

sections.title: Your complete formula toolkit

board_events.text: The whole chapter's formula toolkit
One habit ties it together: work in kelvin, budget the heat, think in ratios.

segments.text: This is your complete toolkit for the whole chapter — a fast restatement, not a re-teach.
Expansion: delta L equals alpha L naught delta T, with beta two alpha and gamma three alpha; density falls as one minus gamma delta T; and thermal stress is Y alpha delta T.
Calorimetry: Q equals m c delta T for a temperature change, Q equals m L for a phase change, and heat lost equals heat gained.
Conduction: H equals K A delta T over L, resistance L over K A, adding in series and adding reciprocals in parallel.
Radiation: net power e sigma A times T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, Wien's lambda m T equals b, and Newton's cooling minus d T by d t equals k times the excess.

Gases: P one V one over T one equals P two V two over T two, the ideal-gas equation P V equals n R T, and the gas thermometer T equals two seventy three point one six times P over P at the triple point.
And change of state: Q equals m L again, with the Clausius-Clapeyron slope d P by d T equals L over T delta V.
<whisper> One habit ties the whole chapter together: work in kelvin, budget the heat before you commit, and think in ratios.
यह पूरे chapter की आपकी complete toolkit है — तेज़ restatement, दोबारा पढ़ाना नहीं।
Expansion: delta L बराबर alpha L naught delta T, beta दो alpha और gamma तीन alpha; density one minus gamma delta T से घटती है; और thermal stress है Y alpha delta T।
Calorimetry: temperature change के लिए Q बराबर m c delta T, phase change के लिए Q बराबर m L, और खोई heat बराबर पाई heat।
Conduction: H बराबर K A delta T over L, resistance L over K A, series में जुड़ती और parallel में reciprocals जुड़ते।
Radiation: net power e sigma A गुना T to the fourth minus T naught to the fourth, Wien's lambda m T बराबर b, और Newton's cooling minus d T by d t बराबर k गुना excess।
Gases: P one V one बटा T one बराबर P two V two बटा T two, ideal-gas equation P V बराबर n R T, और gas thermometer T बराबर two seventy three point one six गुना P बटा P triple point पर।
और change of state: फिर Q बराबर m L, Clausius-Clapeyron slope d P by d T बराबर L over T delta V के साथ।
<whisper> एक आदत पूरे chapter को जोड़ती है: kelvin में काम करो, commit करने से पहले heat budget करो, और ratios में सोचो।

sections.title: One-screen chapter revision

board_events.text: One-screen revision
Heat is not temperature; expansion 1:2:3; gamma=3alpha; water densest at 4 C.
Calorimetry: Warm-Melt-Warm-Boil-Warm; never assume the final state; count the calorimeter.
Conduction: treat as a DC circuit; the poor conductor hogs the drop; ice growth as x squared.
Radiation: power to the fourth in kelvin; hotter is bluer; black absorbs and emits all.
Thermometry: dilute gases agree; absolute zero unreachable; combine as PV/T constant.
Change of state: squeeze ice and it melts; triple point = three phases; evaporation cools.
Grand mnemonic: solids conduct, fluids convect, vacuum only radiates.

segments.text: Finally, the one-screen revision — every subtopic in a single breath.

Temperature and expansion: heat is not temperature; expansion goes one, two, three for line, area, volume; gamma is three alpha; thermal stress is Y alpha delta T; and water is densest at four degrees.
Calorimetry: the five legs are warm, melt, warm, boil, warm; never assume the final state, budget the heat first; and always count the calorimeter.
Conduction: treat every problem as a direct-current circuit; the poor conductor hogs the temperature drop; and ice-growth time scales as thickness squared.
Radiation: power goes as the fourth power in kelvin; hotter is bluer; and a black body absorbs all and emits all.
Thermometry: dilute gases all agree, so they set the standard; absolute zero is unreachable; and combine every gas law as P V over T constant.
Change of state: squeeze ice and it melts; the triple point is where all three phases meet; and evaporation cools while boiling needs heat.
And the grand mnemonic for the three modes of heat transfer: solids conduct, fluids convect, vacuum only radiates. That is the whole chapter.
आख़िर में, one-screen revision — हर subtopic एक साँस में।
Temperature और expansion: heat, temperature नहीं; expansion चलता है one, two, three — line, area, volume; gamma है three alpha; thermal stress Y alpha delta T; और पानी four degrees पर सबसे dense।
Calorimetry: पाँच legs हैं warm, melt, warm, boil, warm; final state कभी मत मानो, पहले heat budget करो; और calorimeter हमेशा गिनो।
Conduction: हर problem को direct-current circuit मानो; poor conductor temperature drop हड़प लेता है; और ice-growth का समय thickness squared की तरह बढ़ता है।
Radiation: power kelvin में fourth power की तरह; ज़्यादा गरम मतलब नीला; और black body सब सोखता और सब उगलता है।
Thermometry: dilute gases सब सहमत, तो वे standard तय करती हैं; absolute zero पहुँच से बाहर; और हर gas law को P V over T constant की तरह combine करो।
Change of state: ice दबाओ तो पिघलती है; triple point वहाँ जहाँ तीनों phases मिलती हैं; और evaporation ठंडक देता है जबकि boiling को heat चाहिए।
और heat transfer के तीन modes का grand mnemonic: solids conduct, fluids convect, vacuum only radiates। यही पूरा chapter है।
